transcripts.title: Engineering Kubernetes for the Next Era of Workloads
transcripts.text:
Good morning, Salt Lake City. I'm Mike Stefaniak, from AWS, and I want to spend the next few minutes talking about what happens when the workloads running on Kubernetes change faster than the assumptions Kubernetes was built on.

For most of its life, Kubernetes grew up with a certain kind of workload in mind. Stateless services. Container images measured in megabytes. Clusters that were large, sure, but large in a way that most of the community could picture. And hardware that was mostly interchangeable: if you needed a GPU, you asked for one, and the scheduler counted them like apples in a basket.

AI changed every one of those assumptions. Container images are now routinely tens of gigabytes, because they carry frameworks, runtimes, and sometimes the model weights themselves. Clusters are approaching a hundred thousand nodes. And accelerators have become something a simple device count can't describe. It matters which GPU you get, what it's connected to, and how close it sits to the network adapter that's going to move data in and out of it.

At AWS, we hit a lot of those limits early, simply because of the scale our customers run at. And when we hit them, we have a choice. We can work around them privately, or we can fix them where everyone benefits. Our answer is that we fix them upstream. So this morning I want to walk through three layers of the stack where that's happened: the container runtime, the control plane, and accelerators.

Let's start at the bottom, with containerd.

When you pull a container image, you're pulling a stack of layers. Each layer has to be downloaded, and then each layer has to be unpacked onto disk before the container can start. For a small image, nobody notices. For an image that's tens of gigabytes, you notice. You notice every time a node comes up, every time you scale out, every time a training job restarts and needs that image on a fresh machine.

When we looked closely at where the time went for large AI images, a lot of it wasn't the network. It was unpacking. Layers were being unpacked one after another, so even when the downloads had finished, you were still waiting on a serial process to grind through the decompression and extraction. That was the long pole.

So we worked in containerd to unpack layers in parallel. Instead of treating unpack as a strictly sequential step, containerd can now do that work concurrently, putting the CPU and disk on a node to work on the actual bottleneck. The effect is that the long pole comes out of pulling large images. And because this lives in containerd itself, it isn't an AWS feature. It's available to anyone running containerd, on any cloud or on their own hardware.

That's the node. Now let's move up to the control plane.

When you push a cluster toward a hundred thousand nodes, you find out very quickly which parts of the control plane were quietly assuming they'd never have to deal with that. A design decision that's invisible at a thousand nodes becomes the thing that falls over at a hundred times that. Usually the culprit isn't a dramatic algorithmic failure. It's contention: many things trying to touch the same piece of shared state at the same time, and waiting on each other to do it.

The first place we went after this was the API server watch cache. The watch cache is how the API server serves the enormous volume of watches that controllers, kubelets, and everything else in the cluster depend on to see changes. At very large scale, lock contention in that cache became a real limiter. Requests weren't slow because there was too much work to do. They were slow because they were queuing for a lock. We removed that contention.

The second place was the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler. The HPA is one of the most widely used pieces of Kubernetes, and it had its own lock contention problem that showed up as clusters and the number of autoscaled workloads grew. We removed that too.

The third was in the scheduler. In any scheduler there's a hot path, the code that runs again and again for every pod, every scheduling cycle. If something on that path is more expensive than it needs to be, you pay for it on every single decision, and at scale those costs compound. We found and fixed one of those hot path issues.

All three of these changes are in Kubernetes 1.37. I want to underline that, because none of it is a special build or a fork. If you run Kubernetes 1.37, you get these improvements, whether your cluster has a hundred nodes or is heading toward a hundred thousand. Smaller clusters may never have felt these limits, but the headroom is there for everyone.

Now let's go to the third layer, and to me this is where it gets most interesting: accelerators.

For a long time, the way you asked Kubernetes for a GPU was to ask for a number. One GPU. Eight GPUs. That model was simple and it got us a long way. But for modern AI workloads, a number doesn't capture what you actually need. Topology matters. Training and inference jobs move a lot of data between the accelerator and the network, and the performance you get depends on whether the GPU and the network adapter sit close together on the hardware, on the same PCIe root, or far apart with extra hops in between.

A device count can't express that. So you'd end up with pods that got the right number of GPUs on paper and still underperformed, because of where those GPUs were relative to the network.

This is what Dynamic Resource Allocation, DRA, is for. With DRA, a pod can describe what it needs in much richer terms than a count. It can say: I need a GPU and a network adapter, and I need them on the same PCIe root. Kubernetes can then allocate devices that actually satisfy that constraint, instead of hoping it works out.

That solves the problem when the right node already exists in your cluster. But in a lot of real environments, especially elastic ones, the node you need doesn't exist yet. It has to be provisioned. And that's where a lot of autoscaling approaches fall down, because to provision the right machine, you have to understand the request well enough to know which machine would satisfy it.

So we've made Karpenter able to provision for DRA requests, including for nodes that don't exist yet. When a pod shows up asking for a GPU and a network adapter on the same PCIe root, Karpenter can reason about that requirement and bring up capacity that will meet it. The scheduling intent and the provisioning decision finally speak the same language.

Put those three layers together and you get a picture of what Kubernetes needs to be for this next era. Nodes that can start large images without unpacking being the bottleneck. A control plane that doesn't choke on contention as clusters grow toward a hundred thousand nodes. And an accelerator model that understands topology, both when it schedules and when it provisions.

I want to close on the part of this I care about most, which is how it happened. Every piece I talked about today landed upstream: in containerd, in Kubernetes itself, and in Karpenter. That's deliberate. The workloads driving these changes aren't unique to any one company or any one cloud. The limits we hit first, many of you are going to hit next, if you haven't already. The best thing we can do is make sure that when you get there, the fix is already waiting for you in the open-source project you're running.

And the work isn't finished. AI workloads are going to keep pushing on assumptions we haven't even noticed we're making yet. When they do, I hope we'll keep doing what this community does best: find the limit, understand it, and fix it upstream, together.

Thank you, and enjoy the rest of KubeCon.

transcripts.title: Pods in the Wild: Reinforcement Learning on Kubernetes with OpenRL
transcripts.text:
Sunil Arora: Good morning, Salt Lake City! It's great to be here with all of you at KubeCon. I'm Sunil, and I'm joined by my colleague Ravin. We want to start this morning with a riddle. What do wild dolphins, open-weight Gemma models, and Kubernetes have in common?

Ravin Kumar: Pods, of course.

Sunil Arora: Thank you. We'll be here all week. But stick with us, because that joke points at something real, and by the end of these few minutes we hope you'll see why the people in this room are going to shape the next phase of AI.

Ravin Kumar: Let me start with the dolphins, because they're my favorite part of this story. For decades, researchers have been out on the water recording dolphins. They've captured whistles, clicks, and burst pulses, and they've written down which animals made which sounds and what those animals were doing at the time. That's a huge body of acoustic data. It's careful and patient, and it's very specialized. The question that has driven this work for a long time is simple to ask and very hard to answer. Is there structure in those sounds? Can we start to understand what dolphins are saying to each other?

Ravin Kumar: That's where DolphinGemma comes in. DolphinGemma takes an open-weight Gemma model and trains it on that marine acoustic data. The model learns the patterns in dolphin vocalizations, so researchers can explore sequences, look for recurring structure, and generate likely continuations of the sounds. In other words, it's a tool that helps scientists decode dolphin communication. Notice what made that possible. It wasn't the biggest model in the world. It was an open model that researchers could adapt, paired with data that only they had.

Sunil Arora: And we think that pattern is much bigger than dolphins. Across the industry, the AI that actually changes how work gets done keeps showing the same shape. You take open weights that you can study and modify and deploy where you need them. Then you pair them with specialized data from your own domain. Put those two together and you get something a general-purpose model can't give you on its own.

Sunil Arora: Now, I want to be careful here, because this is easy to misread. We are not standing up here to tell you frontier models don't matter. They do. Massive foundation models set the bar for general intelligence. They're remarkable at broad reasoning, at handling open-ended problems, and at working through things nobody anticipated. What we see in the architectures that win is that they don't pick one or the other. They combine them. A large foundation model handles the broad reasoning, and lightweight, task-tuned models handle targeted execution.

Ravin Kumar: Think of it like a team. You have a generalist who can look at a messy problem and figure out the plan. Then you have specialists who each do one thing extremely well, very quickly, and very cheaply. You don't want your generalist doing every repetitive, domain-specific step. And you wouldn't ask your specialist to plan the whole project. The combination is what makes it work.

Sunil Arora: So here's our claim. Frontier models will keep pushing general intelligence forward. But the next major operational leap belongs to everyday builders. It belongs to the platform engineers, the SREs, and the application developers in this room. The opportunity is to let practitioners fine-tune open-weight models so they outperform massive frontier baselines on domain-specific tasks, at a fraction of the cost, the footprint, and the latency.

Ravin Kumar: Each of those three matters. Cost decides whether you can run something at scale or only in a demo. Footprint decides where you can run it, whether that's in your own cluster, at the edge, or close to your data. And latency decides whether it feels like part of your application or like waiting on a phone call.

Sunil Arora: So if that's the opportunity, what's been in the way? One of the most powerful techniques for steering a model toward mastering a specific task is reinforcement learning. Instead of only showing a model examples of right answers, you let it attempt the task, you evaluate how well it did, and you use that signal to guide it toward better behavior. When you care about a model getting a particular job right, that loop is incredibly effective.

Ravin Kumar: But historically, reinforcement learning has been trapped. It lived inside elite research labs. It ran on brittle, complex runtimes that were often stitched together for one experiment and hard to reproduce for the next. You needed deep machine learning expertise just to get the loop running, never mind running it reliably. If you were a builder with a real problem and a good dataset, the honest answer was usually that this wasn't for you.

Sunil Arora: And that's a familiar story for this community, isn't it? Think about where we were before Kubernetes. Running distributed systems reliably was a specialist skill. Everyone had their own fragile scripts and their own way of scheduling work, recovering from failure, and scaling up and down. Then this community built a common foundation. We made the hard parts declarative, portable, and shared. We took something that belonged to a few experts and made it something every team could do.

Ravin Kumar: Which brings us to OpenRL. OpenRL is a new CNCF sandbox project, and its goal is to democratize reinforcement learning by bringing it directly onto Kubernetes. The idea is to take RL out of the lab and put it where so many of you already run your workloads.

Sunil Arora: Here's the experience we're aiming for. A builder articulates a task. You say what you want the model to get good at. You point to a dataset, the specialized data that only you have, like the researchers with their recordings. Then you use cloud native technologies to guide an open-weight model toward mastering that task. You don't need to be a reinforcement learning researcher to do it.

Ravin Kumar: And because it's on Kubernetes, you get to bring everything you already know. The scheduling, the scaling, the observability, the way you manage resources and isolate workloads all carry over. Reinforcement learning involves a lot of moving parts that have to work together. Kubernetes is very good at coordinating moving parts. That's the whole point of it.

Sunil Arora: So the riddle wasn't only a pun. The dolphins swim in pods, our workloads run in pods, and the models those workloads train are how we're starting to understand those dolphins. The thread connecting all of it is open models, specialized data, and infrastructure that ordinary builders can actually use.

Ravin Kumar: I keep coming back to the researchers on the water. They didn't need the largest model ever built. They needed a model they could shape to their own data and their own question. There are thousands of questions like that inside your organizations. Most of them aren't about dolphins, but they're just as specific and just as valuable to the people who care about them.

Sunil Arora: OpenRL is a sandbox project, which means it's early, and that's exactly why we're telling you about it here. This community is good at taking early ideas and turning them into durable infrastructure. We'd love for you to try it, tell us where it's rough, and help shape where it goes. Bring your use cases and your datasets, and bring your opinions too. We know you have them.

Ravin Kumar: Frontier models will keep raising the ceiling. With OpenRL, we'd like builders to be the ones raising the floor, so that every team can teach a model to master the task in front of it.

Sunil Arora: Thank you, KubeCon. Enjoy the rest of the show.

transcripts.title: Sandbox Your Agents
transcripts.text:
Good morning, Salt Lake City! It's wonderful to be here with all of you. I want to start with a quick show of hands. How many of you have used an AI agent to write, test, or ship code in the last month? Keep them up if you've let one of those agents run commands in a real environment. Now keep them up if you know exactly what that agent had access to while it was running. Yeah. That's what I thought. And honestly, that's why I'm up here this morning.

AI agents are some of the most powerful automation tooling we've ever had for software development. They can scaffold a service, write the tests, open the pull request, and if we let them, push it all the way through to production before we've finished our coffee. That speed is real, and I don't think any of us want to give it up. But with unfettered power comes some pretty great headaches. The question I keep hearing from teams across this community isn't "should we use agents?" It's "how on earth do we scope and secure them inside our cloud native stacks?"

Let's be honest about what goes wrong. An agent is, at its core, a process that takes instructions, makes decisions, and executes actions. When we hand it credentials, it uses them. When we give it a shell, it runs commands in that shell. And it doesn't always understand the blast radius of what it's doing. A problematic agent with too much access can take down an entire production stack. It can wipe a database. Sometimes that happens because someone deliberately granted it broad permissions to get a demo working, and that demo quietly became the real workflow. Sometimes it happens because nobody fully understood what access was being inherited. The agent picked up a kubeconfig sitting in a home directory, or an environment variable with a cloud token in it, and suddenly the thing you asked to fix a flaky unit test is talking to your production cluster.

None of this is malicious. That's the uncomfortable part. Most of these incidents come from choices made under deadline pressure, or from a simple lack of knowledge about what the agent can actually reach. So the answer can't be "just be more careful." We've been in this industry long enough to know that "be more careful" isn't a security model. The answer has to be structural. We have to build environments where the agent cannot do the dangerous thing, even when it tries, even when it's confused, and even when the person running it didn't think it through.

The good news is that this community has spent over a decade building the exact primitives we need. We already know how to isolate workloads. We already know how to give a process its own filesystem, its own network view, and its own identity. We already know how to declare what something is allowed to do and have the platform enforce it. Containers, namespaces, network policies, role-based access control, admission control, short-lived credentials: none of this is new. What's new is the kind of workload we're pointing it at. My argument this morning is simple. An agent is a workload, and we should treat it like one. Specifically, we should treat it like an untrusted one.

So what does that look like in practice? Start with the sandbox itself. Every agent task should run in its own containerized environment, created for that task and thrown away when it's done. Not a long-lived developer VM that slowly accumulates credentials and state. Not your laptop. A fresh, ephemeral sandbox with exactly the tools, source code, and permissions that task requires and nothing more. If the agent needs to run your test suite, it gets the repository and the test dependencies. It doesn't get your cloud admin role, and it doesn't get a route to the production database. If it needs to call one internal API, the network policy allows that one API and denies everything else by default.

This is where community building blocks like OpenShell come in. The point of a project like this is to give agents a place to operate that is scoped by design. The agent gets a shell, because agents need to run commands to be useful, but that shell lives inside a boundary that you defined ahead of time. What it can see, what it can execute, and where it can reach are decisions you make declaratively, not things you discover after the fact. That shift from discovering access to declaring access is the whole game.

Now, isolation from your production systems is one half of the problem. The other half is isolation from everything else around the agent, including, in some cases, the infrastructure it runs on. Agents work with sensitive material: proprietary source code, customer data in test fixtures, secrets they need to complete legitimate tasks. When you run that at scale on shared infrastructure, you have to ask who else can see inside that sandbox. That's the problem Confidential Containers is designed to address. By running workloads inside hardware-backed trusted execution environments, Confidential Containers lets you protect the data and code inside a sandbox even from the host it's running on. And through attestation, you can verify that the environment is what it claims to be before you release secrets into it. For agentic workloads that's a powerful combination. You can say: this agent only gets the credentials it needs, and only after we've confirmed it's running in an environment we trust.

Put those pieces together and you get layers. Ephemeral, containerized sandboxes keep each agent task contained and disposable. Scoped shells and policy define exactly what the agent can do inside that boundary. Confidential computing protects what's inside the sandbox from the outside world. And the orchestration we all already know lets you run this not just for one developer on one afternoon, but across your whole organization, at scale.

I also want to be clear that this isn't finished. There's a lot of emerging technology across the cloud native ecosystem tackling different parts of this: how agents get identity, how we audit what they did, how we express intent-based policy that a human can actually read and reason about. Some of it is early. Some of it will change shape over the next year. That's fine. That's how this community has always worked. We build the primitives in the open, we argue about them in issues and working groups, and we converge on patterns that everyone can use.

That last part, everyone, matters most to me. Securing agents can't be something only the largest platform teams can afford to do. If the safe path requires a dedicated security engineering group and six months of custom tooling, most teams will take the unsafe path, because the unsafe path is right there and it works today. Our job as a community is to make the sandboxed path the easy path. It should be the default template. It should be what happens when you just follow the getting-started guide.

So here's what I'd ask of you this week. Go back to that show of hands from the beginning. If you weren't sure what your agents had access to, make finding out your first step. Then try running one workflow, just one, inside a proper sandbox. Look at projects like Confidential Containers and OpenShell. Join the conversations happening here at KubeCon, in the hallway, in the project pavilion, and in the working groups afterwards. Bring your use cases and your failure stories, because the failure stories are how we learn where the boundaries need to be.

Agents are going to keep getting more capable. That's exciting. Let's make sure that as they get more powerful, the boxes we put them in get stronger too. Thank you, and enjoy the rest of KubeCon.
